title: "Leverage Score and SVD"

## Motivation

Working with large single-cell datasets can be computationally expensive. To reduce computational complexity, we can select a representative subset of cells using **leverage score sampling**.

Consider the matrix:

$$
X =
\begin{pmatrix}
10 & 0 \\
10 & 0 \\
10 & 0 \\
0 & 10
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Each row represents a cell, and each column represents a gene.

The first three cells are identical, while the fourth represents a different expression pattern.

If we want to retain only two cells, it would be reasonable to select one of the first three cells and the fourth cell.

**Main idea:** Use Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify the contribution of each cell to the linear structure of the dataset.

## 1. Singular Value Decomposition

Any real matrix can be decomposed as:

$$
\boxed{X = U\Sigma V^T}
$$

where:

- $U$ contains the left singular vectors.
- $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix containing singular values.
- $V$ contains the right singular vectors.

### Step 1: Computing the singular values

Calculate:

$$
X^TX
$$

Find its eigenvalues:

$$
X^TXv_i=\lambda_i v_i
$$

The singular values are:

$$
\boxed{\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}}
$$

Arrange these values in decreasing order along the diagonal of $\Sigma$.

### Step 2: Computing V

The columns of $V$ are the normalized eigenvectors of $X^TX$, ordered according to the singular values.

$$
V=(v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_r)
$$

### Step 3: Computing U

Using:

$$
XV=U\Sigma
$$

we obtain:

$$
\boxed{U=XV\Sigma^{-1}}
$$

for the nonzero singular values.

## 2. Computing leverage scores

For the rank-$k$ approximation, take the first $k$ columns of $U$.

The leverage score of cell $i$ is:

$$
\boxed{\ell_i=\sum_{j=1}^{k}U_{ij}^{2}}
$$

This is the squared Euclidean norm of row $i$ of $U_k$.

A high leverage score indicates that the cell contributes strongly to the selected singular subspace.

## 3. Sampling cells

We can use leverage scores to define sampling probabilities:

$$
\boxed{p_i=\frac{\ell_i}{\sum_j \ell_j}=\frac{\ell_i}{k}}
$$

Cells with higher leverage scores are more likely to be selected.

This helps preserve important directions of variation and can improve the representation of rare cell populations.

However, rare cells are not guaranteed to have high leverage scores, especially if their characteristic directions are excluded from the rank-$k$ approximation.
